liturgical_day: Wednesday of the Thirty-third Week in Ordinary Time
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: Trade until I come
theme: The gift is entrusted to us for use.
introduction: Near Jerusalem, the listeners expect the kingdom to appear immediately. Jesus tells them of a nobleman who leaves his servants with money and returns to ask what they have done with it. Eusebius reads the interval through Christ’s Ascension and return. Theophylact hears a warning for every recipient of grace: gifts can grow through use, or wither through neglect.
hero_alt: A nobleman entrusts a silver coin to a servant in a stone courtyard, with Jerusalem in the distance, in gold Byzantine mosaic and deep blue stained glass.
closing_title: What has been put into our hands?
closing: Theophylact names prayer, fasting, gentleness, and humility among the gifts that require our care. He reads the parable as a call to keep using what God gives. The gift wrapped away remains unfruitful; the gift put to use can grow.
copyright_notes: Scripture is an original modernization of the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible, not of the USCCB or Vatican News Lectionary wording. All eighteen verses of Luke 19:11–28 are included, including the abundance clause in verse 26 and the severe judgment in verse 27. Pounds denotes the ancient mina, not modern currency. Official dated sources establish the date, title, and citation only. Insights and expansions are original summaries of the public-domain Newman translation of the Catena Aurea, not verbatim quotations. Allegorical readings are commentary, not additions to Scripture. Augustine’s comment on verse 14 describes historical resistance to apostolic preaching, not collective inherited guilt. Chrysostom’s comment on verse 27 concerns divine judgment and the unity of Father and Son, not a command for readers to commit violence.

verses.text: As they were hearing these things, he added a parable, because he was near Jerusalem and because they thought that the kingdom of God would immediately be revealed.
verses.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
verses.insight: The miracles have raised expectations of an immediate kingdom. Eusebius says Jesus prepares his hearers for his departure to the Father.
verses.commentary: Eusebius begins with the expectation surrounding Jesus as he approaches Jerusalem. Those who have witnessed his divine miracles suppose that his kingdom will begin at his first coming. They expect its appearance soon, with the journey to the city. Jesus therefore gives them a different account of what lies ahead. He will leave mankind and go to his Father before receiving the kingdom. In Eusebius's reading, the parable corrects their timetable by setting his departure between the present ministry and the kingdom they are expecting.
verses.source_label: Eusebius of Caesarea, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: He said therefore: A certain nobleman went to a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself, and to return.
verses.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
verses.insight: Eusebius reads the journey as Christ’s Ascension and the return as his coming again in glory.
verses.commentary: Eusebius understands the nobleman's journey to a distant country as the Saviour's Ascension from earth to heaven. Receiving a kingdom and returning point forward to his second appearance as King in glory. The description begins with a man because Christ has truly been born in the flesh. His nobility belongs to the same account of who he is, while the royal return lies ahead. Eusebius connects the promised kingdom with Daniel's vision of the Son of Man receiving dominion. The departure does not end his relationship with those he leaves.
verses.source_label: Eusebius of Caesarea, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: And calling his ten servants, he gave them ten pounds and said to them: Trade until I come.
verses.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
verses.insight: The equal coins signify a shared stewardship. Eusebius identifies the work as preaching the one faith entrusted to the disciples.
verses.commentary: Eusebius identifies the servants with Christ's disciples. Each receives a pound because each is entrusted with the same stewardship. The work commanded during the master's absence is the preaching of his kingdom to those willing to hear. Eusebius stresses the unity of what they proclaim: one doctrine, one faith, one baptism. The equal gift expresses that common trust. Though the servants will later report different gains, the teaching they have received is the same. Their task is to put it to use among hearers until the Lord returns.
verses.source_label: Eusebius of Caesarea, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: But his citizens hated him, and they sent a delegation after him, saying: We will not have this man reign over us.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: Augustine relates the delegation to opposition that continues after the Resurrection, when the apostles preach the Gospel.
verses.commentary: Augustine reads the message sent after the nobleman as opposition to Christ that continues after his Resurrection. He points to the persecution of the apostles and the refusal of their Gospel preaching. The word 'after' matters in his reading: Christ's departure does not bring that resistance to an end. The rejection now encounters the messengers who proclaim him. Augustine is explaining the parable through this particular history of resistance to the apostolic mission. His comment concerns those who refuse the preaching, rather than the servants who receive and use their master's gift.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: And it came to pass that he returned, having received the kingdom; and he commanded the servants to whom he had given the money to be called, so that he might know how much each had gained by trading.
verses.author: Eusebius of Caesarea
verses.insight: The returning king brings the account of Christ’s first coming toward his second. The entrusted servants must now answer for their stewardship.
verses.commentary: Eusebius distinguishes the two comings within the movement of the story. The earlier part has instructed the hearers about the Saviour's first coming; the return of the nobleman now sets before them his second coming in majesty and glory. The kingdom has been received, and the servants are summoned. Eusebius places that summons within the royal return rather than the immediate earthly triumph the listeners had expected. The account follows a period in which the servants have held their master's money and had the opportunity to use it.
verses.source_label: Eusebius of Caesarea, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: And the first came, saying: Lord, your pound has gained ten pounds.
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Cyril sees ministers of the word presenting the fruit of their service. Their praise and reward await Christ’s return.
verses.commentary: Cyril reads the first servant's report in relation to those who minister the word of God. When Christ returns in his kingdom, they receive the praise due to their service and rejoice in heavenly rewards. The increase brought before the master expresses the fruit of what was entrusted to them. Cyril describes their work as multiplying the gift by gaining further gifts. His explanation keeps the report connected to Christ's return: the servants' labor during the interval is brought before the Lord who first gave them their trust.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: And he said to him: Well done, good servant; because you have been faithful in a little, you shall have authority over ten cities.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede identifies faithfulness with keeping God’s word uncorrupted. Present gifts are small beside what is promised.
verses.commentary: Bede explains the servant's faithfulness as a refusal to corrupt the word of God. The entrusted teaching must be handed on without adulteration. He also pauses over the master's description of the trust as very little. This does not make the gift worthless; it places what is received now beside what is still to come. All present gifts are small in that comparison. Bede therefore joins fidelity in teaching to the disproportion between the servant's present stewardship and the far greater reward promised by the returning Lord.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: And the second came, saying: Lord, your pound has gained five pounds.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede reads this servant as the preachers sent to the Gentiles. The fivefold gain signifies people drawn from enslavement to the bodily senses into Gospel faith.
verses.commentary: Bede gives the second servant an allegorical meaning within the Church's preaching. He represents those sent to announce the Gospel to the uncircumcised. The pound is the faith of the Gospel, and its fivefold increase refers to nations formerly enslaved to the five bodily senses. Through preaching, they are converted to the grace of that faith. The numbers belong to Bede's spiritual interpretation of the story. His attention rests on the growth of the Gospel among those outside Israel and on the shared faith entrusted to its preachers.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: And he said to him likewise: You also shall be over five cities.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: For Bede, the reward is bound to the people enlightened by the Gospel. Their faith and conduct become part of the preacher’s glory.
verses.commentary: Bede continues his interpretation of the second servant, whom he associates with the mission to the Gentiles. To be placed over five cities means being exalted through the faith and conduct of the souls enlightened by that preaching. The reward is thus connected with the people brought to Gospel faith. It does not stand apart from the work that produced the increase. In Bede's account, the servant's honor shines through those hearers whose lives have been changed by the teaching entrusted to him.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: And another came, saying: Lord, behold, here is your pound, which I have kept laid away in a cloth.
verses.author: Theophylact of Ohrid
verses.insight: Theophylact notices the cloth’s association with the dead. The unused gift has been left lifeless and unfruitful.
verses.commentary: Theophylact interprets the cloth around the pound through the cloth used to cover the face of a dead person. That association gives the servant's action a severe meaning. The money has been left as something dead, producing nothing. The servant neither puts it to use nor increases it. What appears in his report as careful preservation is therefore exposed as idleness. Theophylact's image draws attention to the condition of the gift while it remains wrapped away: it has been kept, but it has not been allowed to bear fruit.
verses.source_label: Theophylact of Ohrid, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: For I feared you, because you are a severe man: you take up what you did not lay down, and you reap what you did not sow.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede says the servant’s excuse turns against him. His inactivity goes with a proud challenge to his master’s judgment.
verses.commentary: Bede connects the servant's accusation with the judgment that follows. The man presents his fear of a severe master as an excuse for leaving the money unused. Yet Bede says that the excuse becomes a charge against him. He is idle in the work entrusted to him and proud in calling his lord's judgment into question. The description of a demanding master does not explain away his neglect. It supplies the terms on which his own conduct will be examined when the master answers him.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: He said to him: Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant. You knew that I was a severe man, taking up what I did not lay down and reaping what I did not sow.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: The master answers on the servant’s own terms. Bede asks why such fear did not at least move him to act.
verses.commentary: Bede hears the master's answer as an examination of the servant's stated reasoning. If he believed his lord to be hard and exacting, that belief should have stirred him to take care of the property entrusted to him. The expectation of a strict account would make neglect less defensible, not more. Bede therefore reads the judgment as arising from the man's own words. The master does not need to accept inactivity as the natural result of fear. The excuse itself points toward the care the servant failed to take.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: Why, then, did you not put my money in the bank, so that at my coming I might have collected it with interest?
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede reads the bank as hearts ready to receive God’s word. Hearers return its increase through their works and desire to learn.
verses.commentary: Bede identifies the money with the preaching of the Gospel and the word of God. To put it in the bank is to place that word in hearts prepared to receive it. He then describes the return expected from those who hear. They repay what they have received through their works, or through an earnest desire to understand more than they have yet learned from their teachers. This is a spiritual reading of the exchange in the parable. Its concern is the fruitful reception of teaching in the lives of hearers.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: And he said to those who stood by: Take the pound away from him, and give it to the one who has ten pounds.
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Cyril distinguishes the teacher’s work from God’s power. Teachers plant sound words; God makes understanding fruitful.
verses.commentary: Cyril explains the responsibility of teachers alongside the divine work that makes their teaching fruitful. They are to plant wholesome and profitable words in their hearers' minds. Winning those hearers to obedience and giving fruitfulness to their understanding belongs to divine power. This does not release the servant from his task. The man who leaves the gift unused receives condemnation for sloth instead of praise or honor. Cyril places the removal of the pound after this distinction, holding together the teacher's duty to speak and dependence upon God's power.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: And they said to him: Lord, he has ten pounds.
verses.author: Theophylact of Ohrid
verses.insight: Theophylact answers the apparent surprise: the servant who has used his gift well can put a further trust to use.
verses.commentary: Theophylact explains the transfer by looking at what the fruitful servant has already done. He has increased the pound entrusted to him tenfold. Giving him more therefore provides an opportunity for further gain for his lord. The idle servant, by contrast, has made no effort to increase what he received. Taking the unused gift from him allows it to be placed where it will bear fruit. Theophylact's explanation follows the question raised by the bystanders: the existing abundance is connected to demonstrated use of the master's trust.
verses.source_label: Theophylact of Ohrid, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: But I say to you that to everyone who has, more shall be given, and he shall abound; and from the one who has not, even what he has shall be taken away.
verses.author: Theophylact of Ohrid
verses.insight: Theophylact applies this saying to virtues as well as teaching. Gifts grow through watchful practice and die away through neglect.
verses.commentary: Theophylact extends the lesson beyond preaching and the words of God. Moral virtues also come as gracious gifts: one person receives fasting, another prayer, another gentleness or humility. These gifts increase while those who receive them keep watch over themselves. If their care grows cold, the gifts are extinguished. His interpretation of having therefore involves active use. The person who leaves a gift idle loses even what seemed to be possessed, while the fruitful servant receives a further trust that can bring an increase for the Lord.
verses.source_label: Theophylact of Ohrid, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: But as for those enemies of mine who would not have me reign over them, bring them here and kill them before me.
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: Chrysostom reads the severe ending against the Marcionist division between a good Christ and an evil Old Testament God. Father and Son act together in judgment.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom addresses the Marcionists, who set the goodness of Christ against what they called the evil of the God of the Old Testament. He points to this severe command in Christ's own parable as a challenge to that division. He compares it with the Father sending an army against the vineyard: both Father and Son are described as acting in judgment. His comment concerns their unity, rather than two opposed divine characters. He asks readers to face the words spoken by Christ instead of using Christ's goodness to deny judgment.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:11–27

verses.text: And having said these things, he went ahead, going up to Jerusalem.
verses.author: Titus of Bostra
verses.insight: Titus brings the parable back to Jesus’ journey. He goes toward his Passion after correcting the expectation of an immediate kingdom.
verses.commentary: Titus recalls why those watching Jesus approach Jerusalem had expected the kingdom to begin at once. They had heard him say that the kingdom of heaven was at hand. The parable corrects their misunderstanding and makes clear that the death being plotted against him has not yet been overcome. When he finishes speaking, Jesus proceeds toward his Passion. Titus thus reads the next step of the journey in the light of the teaching just given. The movement toward Jerusalem continues, but its immediate destination is his suffering.
verses.source_label: Titus of Bostra, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 19:28–36
